observation_summary: The test fails with an OutOfMemoryError when processing a large number of points (40,000). The stack trace points to DiagonalMatrix.getData() allocating a large 2D array (double[dim][dim]).
hypothesis: The implementation of DiagonalMatrix.getData() creates a full n x n dense matrix (double[n][n]) regardless of the fact that the matrix is diagonal, leading to an O(n^2) memory allocation that causes an OutOfMemoryError when n is large.
prediction: The DiagonalMatrix.getData() method will be shown to allocate a new double[dim][dim] array, which is unnecessary for a diagonal matrix representation, and this allocation is the direct cause of the heap exhaustion.
experiment_rationale: The stack trace and bug report explicitly identify the memory allocation in DiagonalMatrix.getData() as the source of the OOM. The code snippet confirms the allocation of a full n x n matrix. This is an algorithmic inefficiency where a sparse representation is being converted to a dense one unnecessarily.
reasoning_summary: The bug is an algorithmic inefficiency. The system attempts to represent a diagonal matrix as a dense 2D array, which is O(n^2) in space. For n=40,000, this requires 40,000^2 * 8 bytes ≈ 12.8 GB of heap, which exceeds typical JVM limits. The fix is to avoid this conversion or use a more memory-efficient representation.

alternative_types.why_not_primary: The issue is not a missing capability or design-level omission, but an inefficient implementation of an existing method (getData) that forces a dense representation.
